title: Automatic summary may generate invalid HTML with blockquotes and lists

judge.reasoning:
Both patches fix the reported markdown cases the same way: after the word-count cutoff they scan forward from the wrapper start and extend the summary end until the elements opened before the cutoff are closed. All five independent tests pass on both, and both add unit and integration tests that fail on base. The decisive difference is what happens for the non-markdown formats that go through the same function. For AsciiDoc, reStructuredText and Org, the base code already cuts after the first `` unit, leaving section wrappers like `
` or `
` open. Patch A balances every tag unconditionally, so with those formats the summary would expand to the end of the whole first section, and for a single-section document to the entire content (its scanner returns `sc.pos` when the stack empties exactly at `maxHigh`). That is a real regression in summary length for three supported formats, and Patch A has no test covering it. Patch B explicitly treats div/section/article as containers that do not force expansion, while still including end tags that directly follow the cut (so a markdown blockquote wrapped in a raw `
` is still fully closed). It documents this choice in code and pins it with AsciiDoc, RST and Org section tests plus a quoteblock test. Patch B also reuses the existing golang.org/x/net/html tokenizer, which handles comments, quoted attributes, raw-text elements and case folding for free, and adds simple implied-end handling for repeated `

`/`

  • `. Patch A ships about 120 lines of bespoke tag scanning to cover the same ground; it is reasonably careful (and its fallback to the original cutoff on unbalanced input is arguably safer than B's include-the-rest fallback), but that is a narrow edge case compared with the section regression. Patch A also rewrote the existing benchmark and dropped its correctness assertions, which is unrelated churn. Tests: B's coverage is broader on the issue's scenarios (nested blockquotes, ol, void `
    `, ContentWithoutSummary and Truncated in the integration test) and on the format-specific tradeoff; A's unit tests focus on scanner edge cases. On correctness under realistic inputs, scope discipline and craft, B is the better fix.

title: hugo server: page cut at its previous length when another content file changes in the same batch

judge.reasoning:
Root cause: collectDir dedupes on the walked directory via seenDirs, so when two changed files share a directory the second collectDir call returns early and its file-specific filter never runs; that file is never re-collected and is later rendered with stale metadata against new bytes (hence the old-length cut, U+FFFD, and slice-bounds panic). Both patches address this and both pass all five independent tests, so the decision rests on completeness and robustness.

Patch A changes the dedupe key from directory to path (dirPath.Path()). This is minimal and fixes the reported scenario, but it does so by discarding what the dedupe was for: a batch with N changed files in one directory now walks that directory N times, and overlapping filters (e.g. a structural directory change plus a file change inside it, keyed differently as dir path vs file path) can hand the same file to the rungroup twice. It also leaves a direct variant of the issue broken: fileEventsContentPaths still drops regular files below a leaf bundle, so editing index.md and p1.md of the same bundle in one batch never re-collects p1.md, producing the exact stale-length symptom the issue title describes. A's single test covers grow and shrink only.

Patch B keeps one walk per directory but groups the per-id filters and ORs them, which preserves the dedupe's intent while guaranteeing every changed path's filter is applied. The helper collectDirPath makes the grouping key identical to collectDir's seenDirs key, so nothing can be lost. It also removes the leaf-bundle drop in fileEventsContentPaths, with an accurate comment explaining why (the leaf bundle filter only matches the bundle file in the non-structural case), fixing the index+resource same-batch variant. The closure deferral relies on Go per-iteration loop variables, which modern Hugo requires. B's five tests cover grow (exact match), shrink, edit+add in a batch, two bundle resources, and bundle index+resource, each of which fails on base and passes with the fix. The site.go change is extra scope, but it is the same bug class and is reasoned, not churn.

B is the more complete root-cause fix with stronger tests; A is correct for the headline case but degrades the collector's dedupe and leaves the bundle variant unfixed.

title: tpl/collections: intersect/union/uniq collapse or drop distinct big integers beyond the float64 exact range

judge.reasoning:
Both patches fix the root cause the same way: `normalize` now keys integers exactly (int64/uint64) and only falls back to float for non-integral floats, and `intersector.handleValuePair` uses `hreflect.CompareNumbers` instead of float64 coercion. All independent tests pass on both, so correctness on the issue's own scenarios is equal.

The difference is in what else each patch changes and the risk it carries.

Patch A is tightly scoped. Its only non-number change is a narrow Union tweak that keeps an unconvertible big integer when the result slice is `[]any`. It also uses distinct named key types (`intKey`, `uintKey`, `floatKey`) so normalized numbers cannot collide with the raw `uint64` hashes that `normalize` already emits for uncomparable values; Patch B's `numericKey` returns bare `int64`/`uint64`/`float64`, which reintroduces a (rare) collision path between a big uint and a hashed map/slice that base did not have. A's tests cover in/intersect/union/uniq/complement/symdiff at unit and integration level, including mixed int/uint/float and the exact template from the issue.

Patch B rewrites `handleValuePair` to `hreflect.Indirect` both sides before the switch. That dereferences pointers, so the Pointer/Struct branch now compares `types.Unwrapv(v1.Interface()) == types.Unwrapv(v2.Interface())` on the pointee structs rather than on pointer identity. For Hugo's most common intersect use (`intersect site.RegularPages ...`), the pointees are `*pageState`, which contains slice fields and is not comparable, so this comparison would panic at runtime; even for comparable pointees it silently changes semantics from identity to value equality. The string branch also drops the `ToStringE` coercion, changing cross-type string/number intersect behaviour. B further rewrites Union's conversion logic (changing existing test expectations, e.g. `[]any{1,2} ∪ []int8{2,3}` now yields `int8(3)`) and makes a sizeable rewrite of `where.go`'s `in`/`not in` handling, dropping the float path and the type-mismatch guard. Some of that is arguably an improvement, but it is well beyond the issue's ask and each piece carries regression risk that the issue did not require.

B's tests are good (a thorough exact-number table across all ops plus where tests), roughly on par with A's. But on scope and craft, A delivers the fix with far less risk, and B's intersect change plausibly breaks a core use case. A wins.

title: Build hangs forever after 10 page render errors: `renderPages` blocks on `pages <- p` after `errorCollator` calls `Stop`

judge.reasoning:
Both patches apply the identical root-cause fix: the walker's send becomes `case pages <- p:` inside the select on `s.h.Done()`, so the walk can always exit after `errorCollator` calls `Stop`, and `renderPages` reaches `close(pages)`, `wg.Wait()` and `<-errs`. Independent tests confirm both resolve the hang (both FAIL-ASSERT on base, PASS on A and B), so correctness on the reported scenario is equal.

Patch B goes slightly further in ways the issue itself points at and that reduce risk rather than add it. It buffers `errs` (the issue's own suggestion) so the collator can never block on its final send. More importantly, it fixes the existing early return on `w.Walk` error: on base and on Patch A, a walk error returns before `close(pages)`/`wg.Wait()`, leaving the `pageRenderer` goroutines parked on `<-pages` and the collator parked on `errs` forever. The issue explicitly warns about exactly this class of early return. Patch B's restructuring (capture `walkErr`, always close/wait/drain, then return `walkErr` first) is small, easy to reason about, and preserves the error precedence. This is the kind of edge-case error handling the craft criterion asks for, not unrelated churn.

Tests are near-equivalent: same reproducer (50 pages, GOMAXPROCS=1, NUMWORKERMULTIPLIER=2, 10 iterations with a timeout), both would fail before and pass after. Patch B additionally asserts the collated error mentions the layout path, slightly strengthening the check that errors are actually reported, and lives in the existing build-errors test file next to related tests, with a comment explaining the regression. Patch A creates a new file and uses a tighter 10s timeout, which is marginally more prone to false failures on slow CI. Both share the same minor hazard of mutating process-global GOMAXPROCS in a package with parallel tests, so that is a wash.

Patch B also adds an explanatory comment at the select explaining why the send must select on Done, which helps future readers. Net: equal on the core fix, B better on edge handling and craft with no added risk.

This report was written by Claude Opus 5.5

## What version of Hugo are you using?

```text
hugo v0.168.0-e27a6760c5547237f87d353aebe0580feadb20f4 linux/amd64 BuildDate=2026-10-13T16:42:50Z VendorInfo=gohugoio
```

## Does this issue reproduce with the latest release?

Yes.

## What happened

When a build has 10 or more page render errors, `hugo` sometimes never exits.
It prints no error, uses no CPU, and waits forever. A SIGQUIT dump shows the
page walker in `renderPages` blocked sending to `pages`, and `errorCollator`
blocked on its final send to `errs`. No `pageRenderer` goroutines are left.

The hang is a race. With default settings, the reproducer below hung in 26 of
500 builds on a 16-CPU linux/amd64 machine. With `GOMAXPROCS=1
HUGO_NUMWORKERMULTIPLIER=2` (the script's defaults; they only change
scheduling), it hung in 30 of 30 builds (3 runs of the script, 10 builds each,
about 50 seconds per run).

## Expected

The build fails promptly and prints the collated render errors.

## Reproducer

POSIX shell. It creates a site in `$(mktemp -d)` whose pages all fail to render
(`.Content` on a nil resource), builds it `RUNS` times, treats a build that
doesn't exit within `LIMIT` seconds as hung, and prints the goroutine dump of
the first hung build (`timeout -s QUIT`). It deletes the site when done.

```sh
#!/bin/sh
# Build a site whose pages all fail to render, RUNS times; report builds
# that don't exit within LIMIT seconds and print the first one's goroutines.
HUGO=${HUGO:-hugo}
PAGES=${PAGES:-50}
RUNS=${RUNS:-10}
LIMIT=${LIMIT:-5}
# Scheduling settings that make the race hit almost every time.
# Set both to "" to use Hugo's defaults (the hang is then much rarer).
export GOMAXPROCS="${GOMAXPROCS-1}"
export HUGO_NUMWORKERMULTIPLIER="${HUGO_NUMWORKERMULTIPLIER-2}"

dir=$(mktemp -d) || exit 1
trap 'rm -rf "$dir"' EXIT
trap 'exit 130' INT TERM

site=$dir/site
mkdir -p "$site/layouts" "$site/content"
printf 'disableKinds = ["taxonomy", "term", "rss", "sitemap"]\n' > "$site/hugo.toml"
# .Content on a nil resource: every page fails to render.
printf '{{ (resources.Get "missing.svg").Content }}\n' > "$site/layouts/single.html"
cp "$site/layouts/single.html" "$site/layouts/list.html"
i=1
while [ "$i" -le "$PAGES" ]; do
  printf -- '---\ntitle: p%s\n---\n' "$i" > "$site/content/p$i.md"
  i=$((i + 1))
done

"$HUGO" version
echo "GOMAXPROCS=$GOMAXPROCS HUGO_NUMWORKERMULTIPLIER=$HUGO_NUMWORKERMULTIPLIER PAGES=$PAGES"
hung=0 n=1
while [ "$n" -le "$RUNS" ]; do
  timeout -s QUIT "$LIMIT" "$HUGO" -s "$site" -d "$dir/public" > "$dir/log" 2>&1
  if [ $? = 124 ]; then
    hung=$((hung + 1))
    echo "build $n: hung (no exit after ${LIMIT}s)"
    [ "$hung" = 1 ] && cp "$dir/log" "$dir/first-hang"
  else
    echo "build $n: exited"
  fi
  n=$((n + 1))
done
echo "hung in $hung of $RUNS builds"
if [ "$hung" -gt 0 ]; then
  echo "--- output of first hung build (SIGQUIT goroutine dump) ---"
  cat "$dir/first-hang"
  exit 1
fi
```

Run it with `HUGO=/path/to/hugo sh repro.sh`. For Hugo's default scheduling,
run `GOMAXPROCS= HUGO_NUMWORKERMULTIPLIER= RUNS=500 sh repro.sh`.

The main goroutine waits in `errgroup.(*Group).Wait` in
`commands.(*hugoBuilder).fullBuild`. The other goroutines are idle runtime and
cache goroutines.

## Analysis

Line numbers are for the v0.168.0 tag.

[`hugolib/site_render.go` L91–L104](https://github.com/gohugoio/hugo/blob/v0.168.0/hugolib/site_render.go#L91-L104),
the walk handler in `renderPages`, checks for cancellation only before it
blocks:

```go
select {
case <-s.h.Done():
	return radix.WalkStop, nil
default:
	pages <- p // L98
}
```

[`hugolib/site.go` L1574–L1588](https://github.com/gohugoio/hugo/blob/v0.168.0/hugolib/site.go#L1574-L1588),
`errorCollator`, calls `s.h.Stop()` after `maxErrors` (10) errors (L1583–L1586)
and stops reading `results`. Each `pageRenderer` then sees `Done()` in
`sendErr` on its next error
([`site_render.go` L132–L139](https://github.com/gohugoio/hugo/blob/v0.168.0/hugolib/site_render.go#L132-L139))
and returns, so nothing reads `pages` any more.

If the walker passed its `Done()` check before `Stop()` and is blocked on the
full `pages` channel (buffered to `numWorkers`, L75), the send at L98 never
completes. The walk never returns, so `close(pages)`, `wg.Wait()` and
`err := <-errs`
([L110–L116](https://github.com/gohugoio/hugo/blob/v0.168.0/hugolib/site_render.go#L110-L116))
are never reached. The deferred `errs <- ...` in `errorCollator` (`site.go`
L1577, unbuffered `errs`, `site_render.go` L76) then blocks too, and the
collated errors are never returned or printed.

## Suggested fix

Make the send itself select on `Done()`, so the walker can always leave:

```go
select {
case <-s.h.Done():
	return radix.WalkStop, nil
case pages <- p:
}
```

With that, `renderPages` always reaches `<-errs`, so the collator's final send
completes. Making `errs` buffered (`make(chan error, 1)`) would also stop the
collator goroutine blocking if a future change returns early before L116.

judge.reasoning: Both patches apply the identical root-cause fix: setting sourceFilenameIsHash(true) on the create path of ImageCache.getOrCreate so a processed image's Key() is the same whether it was built fresh or read from the file cache. This issue report was written by Claude Opus 5.5, and checked against Hugo v0.168.0. ### What version of Hugo are you using (`hugo version`)? 
$ hugo version
hugo v0.168.0-e27a6760c5547237f87d353aebe0580feadb20f4+extended linux/amd64 BuildDate=2026-10-13T16:42:50Z VendorInfo=gohugoio
### Does this issue reproduce with the latest release? Yes. It also reproduces with v0.167.0, and the code involved is unchanged on master (77230eb). ### Description When the image passed to `images.Overlay` (or `images.Mask`) was itself processed, the filtered image's file name depends on whether that processed image was created in this build or read from the file cache. With an empty resource cache, build 1 publishes the overlay under one name and build 2 under another. The bytes are identical. From build 2 onwards the name stays the same. Expected: the same name in every build. Actual: one name in the first build after the overlaid image is (re)processed, and a different name in later builds. ### Reproduction ```sh #!/usr/bin/env bash # Usage: ./repro.sh [extra hugo flags, e.g. --gc] set -euo pipefail cd "$(mktemp -d)" mkdir -p assets layouts # 64x64 solid-colour PNG echo 'iVBORw0KGgoAAAANSUhEUgAAAEAAAABACAIAAAAlC+aJAAAATklEQVR42u3PQQkAAAgEsIt20Y1mBN/CYAWWaV+LgICAgICAgICAgICAgICAgICAgICAgICAgICAgICAgICAgICAgICAgICAgICAgMBlAXfcAS0jwTZyAAAAAElFTkSuQmCC' | base64 -d > assets/a.png echo "disableKinds = ['page', 'rss', 'section', 'sitemap', 'taxonomy', 'term']" > hugo.toml cat > layouts/home.html <<'HTML' {{- $a := resources.Get "a.png" -}} {{- $s := $a.Process "resize 32x" -}} overlay={{ ($a | images.Filter (images.Overlay $s 0 0)).RelPermalink }} key={{ $s.Key }} HTML for i in 1 2 3; do ${HUGO:-hugo} --quiet "$@" echo "build $i: $(cat public/index.html)" echo " resources/_gen/images: $(ls resources/_gen/images | tr '\n' ' ')" done (cd public && md5sum a_hu_*.png) ``` Output with v0.168.0: ``` $ ./repro.sh build 1: overlay=/a_hu_41f8c20fc0cc13b7.png key=/a_hu_498f860d9a6e2307.png_2100844135326038661 resources/_gen/images: a_hu_41f8c20fc0cc13b7.png a_hu_498f860d9a6e2307.png build 2: overlay=/a_hu_2068adca79b7981a.png key=/a_hu_498f860d9a6e2307.png resources/_gen/images: a_hu_2068adca79b7981a.png a_hu_41f8c20fc0cc13b7.png a_hu_498f860d9a6e2307.png build 3: overlay=/a_hu_2068adca79b7981a.png key=/a_hu_498f860d9a6e2307.png resources/_gen/images: a_hu_2068adca79b7981a.png a_hu_41f8c20fc0cc13b7.png a_hu_498f860d9a6e2307.png afcf7e427a895667f311c7877366ee4a a_hu_2068adca79b7981a.png afcf7e427a895667f311c7877366ee4a a_hu_41f8c20fc0cc13b7.png $ ./repro.sh --gc build 1: overlay=/a_hu_41f8c20fc0cc13b7.png key=/a_hu_498f860d9a6e2307.png_2100844135326038661 resources/_gen/images: a_hu_41f8c20fc0cc13b7.png a_hu_498f860d9a6e2307.png build 2: overlay=/a_hu_2068adca79b7981a.png key=/a_hu_498f860d9a6e2307.png resources/_gen/images: a_hu_2068adca79b7981a.png a_hu_498f860d9a6e2307.png build 3: overlay=/a_hu_2068adca79b7981a.png key=/a_hu_498f860d9a6e2307.png resources/_gen/images: a_hu_2068adca79b7981a.png a_hu_498f860d9a6e2307.png afcf7e427a895667f311c7877366ee4a a_hu_2068adca79b7981a.png afcf7e427a895667f311c7877366ee4a a_hu_41f8c20fc0cc13b7.png ``` `$s.Key` has a `_` suffix in build 1 and none in build 2. Both overlay files in `public/` have the same MD5. Replacing `images.Overlay $s 0 0` with `images.Mask $s` gives the same pattern: two names, identical bytes. ### Cause - On a file cache hit, `ImageCache.getOrCreate` marks the image with `setSourceFilenameIsHash(true)`. The `create` path just below it does not: https://github.com/gohugoio/hugo/blob/77230eba0469604d28434a8eacee868f3274e6ac/resources/image_cache.go#L67 - `genericResource.Key()` appends `_` only when `!l.sourceFilenameIsHash` (`includeHashInKey` is always true for images, [resource_spec.go#L204](https://github.com/gohugoio/hugo/blob/77230eba0469604d28434a8eacee868f3274e6ac/resources/resource_spec.go#L204)): https://github.com/gohugoio/hugo/blob/77230eba0469604d28434a8eacee868f3274e6ac/resources/resource.go#L465 - `Overlay` and `Mask` put the other image's `Key()` into the filter options, and the filter options feed into the output name: https://github.com/gohugoio/hugo/blob/77230eba0469604d28434a8eacee868f3274e6ac/resources/images/filters.go#L51 https://github.com/gohugoio/hugo/blob/77230eba0469604d28434a8eacee868f3274e6ac/resources/images/filters.go#L59 ### Impact - The overlay is processed a second time in build 2, under its new name. - With `--gc`, build 2 deletes the build-1 file, so the cache only settles on the second build after a processed overlay source changes. - The published URL depends on the state of the resource cache. Two builds of the same commit, one with a warm cache and one with a cold cache, publish the same bytes under different URLs. That causes needless uploads on deploy and churns CDN caches. ### Possible fix Making the key of a processed image the same whether it was created in this build or read from the cache would fix this, for example by setting the flag in both paths, or by having `Overlay`/`Mask` use a key that does not depend on where the image came from. Note that `sourceFilenameIsHash` also affects `Publish()` (resource.go#L513), so the first option may have other effects. I have not tested either option. Related: #8066 (which image's name an overlay's output takes; it does not cover this instability) and #11856 (a processed image's name differing after a cache read, now closed).

Both patches fix the reported failure and pass all three independent tests, so the decision rests on where the fix lives and on test quality.

Its integration test covers only the extensionless case with no negative or control case. The semantics B chooses are defensible, but A resolves the issue with less change to a security-relevant contract and with more thorough tests, so A is the better fix.
